question: What do we call skin changes that show up directly as the very first sign of a disease process?
explanation: Spotting primary lesions helps you catch skin conditions right at the beginning before they change. You've got this! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h1)

question: Why is good lighting so important when checking a patient's skin?

options.A: To accurately observe subtle changes in color and moisture
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling nervous during the exam
options.C: To warm up the skin surface before touching it
options.D: To make the physical examination finish much faster

explanation: Great lighting is your best friend! It helps you spot tiny color shifts and moisture levels so you never miss a detail. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h1)

question: What is a flat, colored spot on the skin that is less than 1 cm wide called?
explanation: Think of a simple freckle or flat mole—that's a macule! It's just a flat, colored spot on the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h2)

question: How can you easily tell the difference between a vesicle and a bulla?

options.A: A vesicle contains pus while a bulla contains clear serum only
options.B: A vesicle appears on mucous membranes while a bulla appears on nails
options.C: A vesicle is smaller than 1 cm while a bulla is larger than 1 cm
options.D: A vesicle is solid and raised while a bulla is completely flat

explanation: Both are fluid-filled blisters! The only real difference is their size—bullae are just the bigger ones over 1 cm. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h2)

question: Which secondary skin lesion looks like a narrow crack going down into the skin layer?
explanation: Picture chapped lips or dry, cracked heels—that's a fissure. It's a sharp, linear crack in the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h3)

question: What causes skin to become thick, rough, and leathery, a condition we call lichenification?

options.A: A sudden bacterial infection inside a hair follicle
options.B: Rapid accumulation of watery fluid underneath a bulla
options.C: Chronic scratching and rubbing over a long period
options.D: Exposure to intense ultraviolet sunlight without protection

explanation: When a patient keeps scratching the same spot over and over, the skin fights back by getting thick and leathery. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h3)

question: What do we call those tiny, pinpoint red or purple spots caused by tiny bleeding vessels under the skin?
explanation: Petechiae are those little pinpoint spots that show up when tiny blood vessels (capillaries) leak a bit of blood. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h4)

question: Why don't petechiae and purpura turn white when you press your finger on them?

options.A: Blood has leaked entirely outside the blood vessels into the tissue
options.B: The underlying capillaries are permanently dilated from heat
options.C: The skin has become too thick from chronic scratching
options.D: There is an overproduction of clear serum inside the blister

explanation: Since the red blood cells have escaped right out into the skin tissue, pressing on top won't make the color go away. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h4)

question: What is the clinical term for an uncomfortable skin feeling that makes you really want to scratch?
explanation: Pruritus is just the medical word for itching! You'll see it all the time in clinical notes. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h5)

question: Why should nurses worry when a patient has severe, ongoing itching?

options.A: It proves that the topical medication is working effectively
options.B: It always indicates that a patient has systemic kidney failure
options.C: Scratching breaks the skin barrier and increases infection risk
options.D: It prevents the formation of primary lesions like macules

explanation: The itch-scratch cycle damages the skin's natural defense shield, making it super easy for germs and bacteria to get in. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h5)

question: Which skin sign strongly points to a liver problem or high bilirubin levels?
explanation: Jaundice gives the skin and eyes a yellowish tint because bilirubin is building up in the body. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h6)

question: A patient comes in with a sudden, all-over body rash and a high fever. What should you as a nurse suspect first?

options.A: A potential systemic infection or drug reaction
options.B: A localized injury from scratching a simple insect bite
options.C: A normal physiological change due to aging skin
options.D: A benign primary lesion that requires no follow-up

explanation: When a rash is all over the body AND comes with a fever, it's usually a sign that something is going on inside the whole body, not just the skin. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h6)

question: What is the best way to write down a skin problem in a patient's nursing chart?

options.A: Write the single word 'rash' to save precious time
options.B: Provide precise dimensions, color, and anatomical location
options.C: Guess the exact disease name without checking physical signs
options.D: Record only what the family members report about the spots

explanation: Be specific! Writing down exact measurements, colors, and where it is on the body helps the whole healthcare team track changes accurately. [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h7)

question: Why is it so helpful to note the exact pattern and layout of skin lesions?

options.A: It helps identify specific disease patterns and tracks treatment response
options.B: It proves that secondary lesions always turn into primary lesions
options.C: It eliminates the need to record vital signs during the shift
options.D: It guarantees that the patient will stop scratching immediately

explanation: Many skin conditions have a signature look or layout. Spotting this pattern makes it much easier to figure out what's wrong and if the treatment is working! [learn more](GNS213_U5_T8#GNS213_U5_T8_h7)
